title: The Cowpens, January 1781: a WarMapper reconstruction
label: 1781 (reconstructed)
about: This is a WarMapper reconstruction, not a period map: no map of 1781 shows this ground. The roads are those Edwin Bearss drew in 1967 as the roads of the battle, laid on the ground by the road the park still keeps, and beyond his sheet the roads of the 1959 survey on the lines Mills's map of 1825 gives. The ground is today's, which the park has kept much as it was; the streams are today's. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.
notes: Inside Bearss's sheet the roads are good to about 25-50 m: his road matches the park's trace to 4 m at the median, and his other roads lie within 20-50 m of the roads of 1959. Beyond it they are roads of 1959 (and, for Tarleton's approach, today's Green River Road), rated low. Bearss shows no other roads, houses or fields; the ground was open woods, pastured, with no undergrowth (S107, p. 8).
credit: WarMapper reconstruction from Bearss, 1967 (National Park Service), the USGS sheets of 1959 and 1975, and Mills, 1825

title: The Carolinas, 1775 to 1781: a WarMapper reconstruction
label: 1775 (reconstructed)
about: This is a WarMapper reconstruction, not a period map. Its lines are those of Henry Mouzon's map of the two Carolinas (1775), laid on today's ground: the rivers and the sea coast fitted to today's courses, which they keep, and the main roads and boundary lines carried with them. Mouzon's map was made for the colonies' trade and land grants, not as a survey: his roads are good to a few kilometres, his up-country less. South Carolina is traced at the level of its main lines; North Carolina (since 27 Nov 2026) only for the ground of the campaign of 1781, from Charlotte and Salisbury to Guilford, Hillsborough, Halifax and the Dan; north of the Dan (36.75 N to 37.6 N) the lines are Fry and Jefferson's map of Virginia (1751): its main rivers and the Great Wagon Road. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.
notes: Rivers and coast good to about 1-2 km where today's river is in Natural Earth; roads and boundaries to 3-5 km; the far north-west to no better than 10 km. In North Carolina nine towns hold the fit, each found again 1.3-6.6 km from its site when left out. Not yet traced: inlets, islands and sounds, swamps, the lesser roads, ferries and fords; in North Carolina the Neuse, the Tar and the sounds (east of 77 W, beyond the sheet), the rivers and roads of the mountains and of the east, and Mouzon's towns other than those named. Guilford Court House is not on Mouzon's map (it was built in 1774): its name is placed where the battle's playback has it. Southern Virginia: Fry and Jefferson's rivers are good to about 1-3 km where today's river is in Natural Earth (the Staunton, Meherrin, Nottoway), the Banister, the Appomattox and the Great Wagon Road to about 5 km; they draw almost no other roads there, and nothing at the Dan ferries of 1781.
credit: WarMapper reconstruction from Mouzon, 1775 (Library of Congress), fitted with Natural Earth; North Carolina checked against Collet, 1770, and southern Virginia from Fry and Jefferson, 1751 (Library of Congress)

title: Guilford Courthouse, March 1781: a WarMapper reconstruction
label: 1781 (reconstructed)
about: This is a WarMapper reconstruction, not a period map. On the battlefield the road, creeks, fences and houses are those Charles Hatch drew for the National Park Service in 1971, laid on the ground by the park boundary; he built them on the British plan of 1781 and on the generals' descriptions. West of his sheet the road to New Garden is the road of the 1951 survey. The ground is today's, much built over outside the park. Everything not drawn as a field was woods. Nothing here has been checked by a historian.
notes: Hatch's lines were picked by eye from his plates (pipeline/recon/guilford_1781.py) and are good to about 75 m: his Hunting Creek lies about 70 m east of today's Richland Creek at the road. The roads west of his sheet are roads of 1951, rated low.
credit: WarMapper reconstruction from Hatch, 1971 (National Park Service) and the USGS sheets of 1951
